```{r}
#| label: fig-correlation-structure
#| fig-cap: "Dependence among specification-level signed standardized statistics. The left panel shows their pairwise correlation matrix under the common sign-flipping transformations. The right panel shows the distribution of the off-diagonal pairwise correlations."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5

# Pairwise correlations --------------------------------------------------

cor_long <- as.data.frame(
  as.table(cor(res$Tspace))
)

names(cor_long) <- c(
  "var1",
  "var2",
  "cor"
)

cor_long <- cor_long |>
  mutate(
    var1_num = as.integer(
      factor(
        var1,
        levels = unique(var1)
      )
    ),
    var2_num = as.integer(
      factor(
        var2,
        levels = unique(var2)
      )
    )
  )


# Correlation matrix -----------------------------------------------------

p_cor_matrix <- cor_long |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = var1_num,
      y = var2_num,
      fill = cor
    )
  ) +
  geom_raster() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(
    limits = c(-1, 1),
    guide = guide_colorbar(
      title = "Correlation",
      direction = "horizontal",
      barwidth = unit(5, "cm"),
      barheight = unit(0.45, "cm")
    )
  ) +
  coord_equal(
    expand = FALSE
  ) +
  labs(
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    title = "Pairwise correlation matrix"
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    plot.title = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5,
      size = 14
    )
  )


# Correlation density ----------------------------------------------------

p_cor_density <- cor_long |>
  filter(
    var1_num < var2_num
  ) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = cor
    )
  ) +
  geom_density(
    fill = "grey70",
    alpha = 0.5
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = cor_desc$median_cor,
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Pairwise correlation",
    y = "Density",
    title = "Distribution of pairwise correlations"
  ) +
  theme_bw(
    base_size = 14
  ) +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(
      hjust = 0.5
    )
  )


# Combine ---------------------------------------------------------------

p_cor_matrix +
  p_cor_density +
  plot_layout(
    widths = c(1.1, 1)
  )
```


# Discussion

Methodologically, PIMMA addresses two complementary inferential levels. The `flipmeta` component provides score-based inference within each meta-analytic specification, while the joint PIMMA resampling scheme extends this inference across specifications, enabling both global testing and multiplicity-adjusted post-selection inference. This distinction is central to the proposed framework because valid inference within individual meta-analyses alone does not address the additional selection problem created by examining an entire multiverse.

The application illustrates how PIMMA separates two questions that are often conflated in multiverse analyses: whether there is evidence against the global null and which individual specifications remain rejectable after multiplicity correction. In the CBT example, all pooled estimates were positive but varied considerably in magnitude. The global null was rejected, while most, but not all, specifications remained significant after step-down max-$T$ correction. The application also illustrates why dependence matters: specifications sharing studies or analytical choices can generate correlated test statistics, and the common sign-flipping distribution allows max-$T$ to exploit this structure. Standard corrections like Holm, which ignore test dependence across specifications, led to a more conservative adjustment, whereas PIMMA's common sign-flipping scheme accounts for this correlation structure to maintain statistical power while controlling the family-wise error rate.

These results should therefore be interpreted primarily as a demonstration of the inferential framework rather than as a definitive reassessment of the clinical efficacy of CBT for depression.

# Limitations and future perspectives

The main limitation of the present extension is the assumption that the meta-analytic dataset consists of independent studies contributing a single effect size to each specification. In practice, meta-analytic data often contain dependent effect sizes arising from multilevel or multivariate structures [@Van-den-Noortgate2013-lu; @Cheung2013-hw]. The current implementation therefore requires dependent effects to be reduced to one study-level estimate before applying PIMMA, as in our application. Recent extensions of the flipscores framework have addressed nested and crossed random-effects structures by adapting the resampling scheme to the dependence among observations [@Andreella2025-nd; @Vesely2026-zj]. Extending PIMMA to these more complex meta-analytic structures is an important direction for future work.

A second limitation concerns the construction of the multiverse itself. PIMMA provides inference conditional on the specifications included, but does not determine which analytical choices should be considered reasonable or equally defensible. Their selection therefore remains a substantive and methodological judgment. In our application, we deliberately considered a limited set of plausible alternatives because the goal was methodological illustration rather than an exhaustive clinical assessment of CBT.

Finally, the proposed sign-flipping tests are asymptotically valid under the regularity conditions described above. Their finite-sample performance therefore remains important, particularly for meta-analyses with few studies or highly unbalanced study contributions. Our simulation study provides initial evidence of adequate Type I error control across the conditions considered, but further work is needed to evaluate performance under more complex forms of heterogeneity, model misspecification, and dependence.

# Conclusion

PIMMA extends post-selection inference to multiverse meta-analysis by combining study-level sign-flipping score tests with joint resampling across analytical specifications. It provides a global test and step-down max-$T$ specification-specific inference while controlling the family-wise error rate and accounting for dependence among overlapping meta-analytic specifications. Simulations showed adequate Type I error control across the conditions considered, and the empirical application illustrated how accounting for dependence prevents the unnecessary conservatism of standard independence-assuming adjustments. PIMMA therefore complements descriptive multiverse meta-analysis by allowing researchers to assess not only how results vary across reasonable analytical choices, but also which inferential conclusions remain supportable after those choices are taken into account.
